name: Bloodletting for acne

card.summary: A historical medical practice of drawing blood to clear skin conditions including acne, based on humoral theory.
card.note: Historical; modern medicine uses therapeutic phlebotomy only for specific blood conditions.

quick.overview:
Bloodletting for acne is a historical practice from the era of humoral medicine, in which physicians drew blood to restore the balance of bodily fluids, with clearer skin as one of the hoped-for results. A British medical text of the heroic-medicine period listed acne among many conditions for which it was recommended.

Its appeal for looks was the idea that skin eruptions reflected excess or impure blood. It is no longer part of acne care, and the topic is documented here as medical history.
quick.how: Historically, a physician or barber-surgeon performed venesection or used leeches as part of broader humoral treatment. This wiki gives no technique.
quick.risks: Bloodletting was criticized after studies in the 1830s by Pierre Louis showed no benefit in pneumonia and fevers. Modern therapeutic phlebotomy is limited to conditions such as hemochromatosis, polycythemia and porphyria cutanea tarda.

lead: Bloodletting was a mainstay of Western medicine from antiquity until the 19th century, based on humoral theory, which held that blood, phlegm, black bile and yellow bile had to be kept in balance.[1] In the 18th-century 'heroic medicine' period, one British text recommended it for numerous conditions, acne among them.[1]

Applied to skin, the idea was that removing blood would cleanse the complexion. William Harvey's 1628 work undermined its theoretical basis, and in the 1830s Pierre Louis showed it was ineffective for pneumonia and fevers, although some physicians defended it into the 1870s and it appears in a 1923 textbook.[1]

A related modern echo is therapeutic phlebotomy for porphyria cutanea tarda, a skin condition, and leeches used for some skin diseases.[1] Online lifters occasionally mention blood donation in other contexts, such as managing blood counts on testosterone therapy, which is not an acne use.[2]

chain: Excess or 'impure' blood thought to cause eruptions
angle.text: Historic physicians recommended it as part of treating acne and other skin eruptions. It is documented here for its history, not as a current acne approach.

infobox: Therapeutic phlebotomy for specific blood conditions

paras: Hippocrates mentioned bloodletting in the 5th century BC, and Galen later made blood the dominant humor and set detailed rules for how much to remove by age, season and illness.[1] The Talmud and Islamic authors such as Ibn Sina in the 11th century also addressed it, and printed surgical manuals like Hans von Gersdorff's 1517 book standardized the technique.[1]

Within humoral theory, an excess of blood was believed to cause fevers and skin eruptions, so removal was thought to cure them. An 18th-century British text recommended it for acne along with herpes and other conditions.[1]

Pierre Louis's 1830s analyses showed no benefit for pneumonia and fevers, and by the early 20th century the practice had faded, though it was still recommended in the 1923 edition of a major textbook.[1] Encyclopedic sources describe bloodletting as pseudoscience when used as a traditional treatment.[1]
No studies found. Therapeutic phlebotomy is used for conditions including hemochromatosis, polycythemia and porphyria cutanea tarda, which is not an acne indication.[1]

timeline.event: Hans von Gersdorff's surgical manual helps standardize venesection.[1]
William Harvey's work on circulation undermines humoral basis.[1]
Pierre Louis shows no benefit in pneumonia and fevers.[1]
Still recommended in a medical textbook edition.[1]
